subject: Pathology
vignette: A 67-year-old man with Barrett esophagus is under surveillance. Biopsy of the salmon-colored segment shows glands lined by cells with marked variation in nuclear size and shape, hyperchromasia, an increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and loss of normal basal-to-apical orientation. The changes involve the entire thickness of the epithelium but the basement membrane appears intact and no invasion is seen.
question: Which of the following best describes this lesion?

options.text: Metaplasia with adaptive reprogramming but no atypia
Severe dysplasia, often progressing to carcinoma in situ
Hyperplasia with increased cell number but preserved architecture
Benign hypertrophy with enlargement of individual epithelial cells
Invasive adenocarcinoma with breach of the basement membrane

explanation_correct: Dysplasia is disordered, precancerous epithelial growth marked by pleomorphism, loss of tissue orientation, and nuclear changes such as increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and clumped chromatin. Mild and moderate dysplasia, which spare part of the epithelial thickness, may regress when the inciting cause is removed, but severe dysplasia involving the full epithelial thickness often becomes irreversible and progresses to carcinoma in situ. With an intact basement membrane and no invasion, this is severe dysplasia rather than invasive cancer.

explanation_incorrect.A: Metaplasia is an adaptive replacement of one mature cell type by another and carries no atypia; the pleomorphism and disorientation here place the lesion beyond metaplasia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hyperplasia increases cell number with an intact, orderly architecture and no atypia, whereas the loss of orientation and nuclear atypia define dysplasia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hypertrophy enlarges individual cells while preserving normal structure and does not produce pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, or loss of polarity.
explanation_incorrect.E: Invasive adenocarcinoma requires tumor cells to penetrate the basement membrane; the basement membrane is intact here, so the lesion is still confined to the epithelium.

educationalObjective: Dysplasia is characterized by pleomorphism, loss of tissue orientation, and nuclear atypia; severe full-thickness dysplasia often progresses to carcinoma in situ, and invasion defines carcinoma.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 55-year-old woman with chronic gastroesophageal reflux has a long-standing segment of Barrett esophagus. Her clinician reviews the natural history of the lesion with her and explains that the change in her distal esophagus began as a response of stem cells to acid exposure and has now progressed to a precancerous state. He emphasizes the importance of continued surveillance.
question: Which of the following sequences best describes the stepwise pathway to malignancy in this patient's esophagus?

options.text: Hyperplasia, then hypertrophy, then atrophy, then neoplasia
Atrophy, then dysplasia, then metaplasia, then neoplasia
Metaplasia, then dysplasia, then malignant transformation
Dysplasia, then metaplasia, then hypertrophy, then neoplasia
Hypertrophy, then metaplasia, then atrophy, then neoplasia

explanation_correct: The adaptations ladder runs from a change in cell size or number (hyperplasia, hypertrophy, atrophy) to a change in cell type (metaplasia) and then to a change in cell type and structure (dysplasia), which with continuing injury becomes neoplasia. In Barrett esophagus, gastric acid drives esophageal squamous epithelium to intestinal mucosa (metaplasia), which with persistent insult progresses to dysplasia and then esophageal adenocarcinoma. Dysplasia is usually preceded by persistent metaplasia or pathologic hyperplasia, which is why chronic reflux with metaplasia mandates surveillance.

explanation_incorrect.B: Hyperplasia and hypertrophy are changes in cell number and size that precede a change in cell type; placing them after metaplasia inverts the ladder, and atrophy is not part of the reflux pathway.
explanation_incorrect.C: Atrophy is a decrease in tissue mass, whereas metaplasia appears first as the adaptive replacement of squamous by intestinal epithelium; the order listed reverses metaplasia and dysplasia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Dysplasia is the later, precancerous step that follows metaplasia; putting dysplasia before metaplasia contradicts the ladder in which dysplasia is usually preceded by persistent metaplasia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hypertrophy is not the first step in Barrett esophagus, and atrophy does not follow metaplasia; the progression is metaplasia followed by dysplasia.

educationalObjective: The classic sequence of chronic epithelial injury is metaplasia, then dysplasia, then neoplasia, as illustrated by Barrett esophagus progressing to esophageal adenocarcinoma.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 47-year-old woman with abnormal uterine bleeding is found to have endometrial hyperplasia. Her physician explains that the extent of disease will determine management. A follow-up biopsy shows that atypical changes affect only the inner half of the endometrial epithelial thickness, and the changes appear to be confined to the epithelium.
question: Which of the following statements about her dysplasia is most accurate?

options.text: Mild to moderate dysplasia may regress if the inciting cause is alleviated
All grades of dysplasia are irreversible and mandate hysterectomy
Dysplasia represents a true adaptive response identical to metaplasia
Dysplasia is defined mainly by an increase in cell size without nuclear change
Dysplasia with an intact basement membrane is equivalent to invasive carcinoma

explanation_correct: Dysplasia is graded by how much of the epithelial thickness shows disordered growth and atypia. Mild and moderate dysplasia, which do not involve the entire thickness of the epithelium, may regress with alleviation of the inciting cause such as unopposed estrogen or an irritant. Severe dysplasia, by contrast, often becomes irreversible and progresses to carcinoma in situ. Because this biopsy shows changes limited to the inner half of the epithelium, regression remains possible if the cause is corrected.

explanation_incorrect.A: Only severe, full-thickness dysplasia is characteristically irreversible; mild and moderate dysplasias can regress, so a blanket statement that all grades require hysterectomy is wrong.
explanation_incorrect.B: Dysplasia is explicitly not considered a true adaptive response; it is disordered, precancerous growth, distinct from the adaptive reprogramming that produces metaplasia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Dysplasia is defined by pleomorphism, loss of tissue orientation, and nuclear changes such as increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and clumped chromatin, not simply by larger cells.
explanation_incorrect.E: A lesion with an intact basement membrane and no invasion is dysplasia or carcinoma in situ; invasive carcinoma requires penetration of the basement membrane.

educationalObjective: Mild and moderate dysplasia may regress when the cause is removed, whereas severe full-thickness dysplasia typically becomes irreversible and progresses to carcinoma in situ.
